answer: The ferry rope is gauged at every crossing, and the wear is stamped on the gauge before the boat may leave the bank. A garden rope bought from a pedlar fails the gauge: at the ridge of the rope the strands must show the ferry's own wear, and a pedlar's rope frays evenly. Forging the gauge means running a ferry for a season, bribing the ferryman and paying 6,200, and the fable stamp on the gauge is read at every landing, so a rope whose wear was never measured is cut.
